dossier.public_summary: The 13-day dip is small and flat-bottomed as a 2.2 Earth-radius planet should be, and it lasts about the right time for a 0.83 solar-radius star. However its depth is not the same: it is about 10x deeper in early sectors than later ones, and that change is highly significant even inside the same pipeline. That stability failure, plus a very low planet-likelihood score and no centroid confirmation, makes a variable background blend or systematics more likely than a steady planet.

reasons.why: depth changes dramatically between sectors (1170 +/-162 ppm in sector 5, 1085 +/-126 ppm in sector 7, 209 +/-82 ppm in sector 32, 152 +/-73 ppm in sector 87), 155.7% change with chi2 69.32 dof 3
variation is real within SPOC 2-min: p_constant 1.5390741087224214e-11 between sectors 5,7,32, not a calibration offset between products (QLP vs SPOC)
independent classifier rates this as planet-unlike (0.08 << 0.5 median, <0.1 threshold where false positives dominate)

no sector with a clear difference image (diff_snr -0.9456 used false) so on-target cannot be shown; combined with extreme depth change the best explanation is systematics/variability/blend, not a steady transiting planet

individual transit properties are planet-like (small, flat-bottomed, no odd/even or secondary and duration fits TIC rad 0.8313 / Gaia FLAME 0.8276) but are outweighed by the strong positive evidence for depth instability; a blended EB or two stars in the aperture can mimic a flat dip while being depth-variable
